name: Who Captured the Money: Platform Advertising at Scale
deck: Meta and Google absorbed the advertising dollars that once funded local newsrooms through scale, targeting precision, and measurement infrastructure that local newspapers cannot match structurally.
core_bet: Local journalism is not dying because the story value disappeared. It's dying because the advertising revenue that funded it migrated to Meta Platforms (3.6B daily active people) and Google/Alphabet (search + YouTube) whose scale, targeting precision, and measurement infrastructure make local newspaper CPMs structurally uncompetitive. The value didn't disappear — it migrated to platforms that have no obligation to fund local civic reporting.

mechanism: For most of the 20th century, local newspapers owned local advertising because they were the only efficient way to reach local audiences at scale. A local business could buy a quarter-page ad in the paper to reach their geographic market. That was the newspaper's revenue stream. Digital platforms destroyed that moat in three ways. First: Meta and Google reached larger, more targeted audiences more cheaply. Meta's 3.6B daily active people and algorithmic targeting mean an advertiser can reach their exact target demographic for pennies compared to the newspaper's cost per impression. Second: measurement became automatic and real-time. Advertisers could see exactly how many clicks, impressions, conversions, and revenue their ad generated — something newspapers never offered. Third: the platforms built self-service tools that let businesses run campaigns without an ad salesman, further cutting cost. A local business that once spent $500/month on newspaper ads could now spend $50/month on Meta ads and reach a better-targeted audience.

The scale and targeting advantage is not a close call. Meta's Q2 2026 financial package is instructive: the company reached 3.6B daily active people, delivered 14% growth in ad impressions year-over-year, achieved 12% growth in average price per ad, and generated $60.8B in quarterly revenue — with AI-optimized ad delivery serving as the core competitive moat. A local newspaper has maybe 50,000 readers, most of them already in their community. Meta has orders of magnitude more reach, and it applies AI recommendation engines to show ads to the most likely buyers. The newspaper can't compete on reach, targeting precision, or measurement. It can only compete on local credibility and community connection — and advertisers don't need credibility to sell local services.

The broader advertising stack reinforced this. Companies like Criteo ($1.3B+ media spend quarterly routed through their commerce platform) and The Trade Desk ($715.1M Q2 2026 revenue managing programmatic advertising infrastructure) emerged to automate and optimize ad buying across fragmented digital channels. These platforms made it possible for advertisers to coordinate campaigns across hundreds of publishers and inventory sources without negotiating direct relationships. That further eroded the local newspaper's value proposition. The newspaper once owned the local advertising channel. Now they're just one fractional inventory slot inside a much larger programmatic marketplace where they're competing against billions of impressions from Meta, Google, and thousands of other publishers worldwide.
why_now: Three converging factors accelerated the advertising capture around 2010-2020. First: mobile devices made it possible for consumers to be reached anywhere, anytime, outside the newspaper. Second: social media created network effects that attracted both users (reaching critical mass) and advertisers (following the users). Third: programmatic advertising infrastructure matured enough that buying ad inventory could be automated and optimized, removing the friction of direct sales relationships. Local newspapers optimized for the print-era model (one salesman, one pitch, one relationship per advertiser) just as the market shifted to algorithmic efficiency at scale. They couldn't respond fast enough.
who_pays: Local communities pay by losing civic oversight. When the newspaper loses advertising revenue, it cuts reporters. When there are fewer reporters, government, courts, and local businesses face less scrutiny. Corruption goes undetected longer. School boards make decisions without coverage. Development deals happen without public awareness. The human cost is invisible until something goes very wrong.
who_profits: Meta and Google profit most directly. They captured the local advertising dollars without any obligation to fund journalism. Criteo and The Trade Desk profit by taking a small cut of advertising budgets flowing through their platforms. Technology companies profit by selling tools that local businesses use to run their own ads instead of hiring local ad salespeople.
tension: The externalized cost is the hollowing of local civic infrastructure. The second tension is that the platforms' algorithm treats all content equally — a quality investigative report is worth the same as a misleading rumor when they're both competing for attention and ad revenue. The third tension is concentration: as local news dies, people have fewer independent sources of information about local issues, making them more vulnerable to misinformation and more dependent on whatever narrative they find on social media.
surprising_part: The most underappreciated fact is that this isn't a business failure by newspaper companies. The Value didn't disappear because the newspaper product got worse. The value disappeared because the structure of advertising itself changed. If a newspaper owner could have run Meta's algorithm on local display ads from 2010, they would have made it work. But they couldn't. The technological and capital requirements to build a Meta-scale platform were beyond what a regional newspaper company could afford or build.
one_sentence: Meta and Google didn't kill local news by running better newspapers — they killed it by offering advertisers a better place to spend money with zero obligation to fund journalism.
societal_stake: Local democratic participation depends on local information. When local newspapers collapse, communities lose the institution that covered school boards, city councils, development disputes, and local corruption. Without that coverage, political participation drops, civic knowledge declines, and communities become more fragmented. The platforms gain advertising revenue and users, but society loses the shared information infrastructure that held local democracy together.
